title: How to Download Your GTBank Statement
titleTag: How to Download Your GTBank Statement (2026)
metaDescription: A step-by-step guide to downloading your GTBank account statement from the GTWorld app or internet banking, and opening the password-protected PDF.
directAnswer: To download your GTBank statement, open the GTWorld app, go to Statements, choose your account and date range, and request an e-statement. GTBank emails it to you as a password-protected PDF, usually within a few minutes.

children.text: Your GTBank statement is the fastest way to see everything that has come in and gone out of your account. Here is how to get it, step by step.
Open GTWorld and sign in, tap Statements (under your account), pick the account and the date range you want, then request the e-statement. It arrives by email as a PDF.
GTBank protects the PDF with a password. Enter it exactly as GTBank specifies to open the file. If you are unsure of the format, check the email GTBank sent with the statement.

commonProblems.solution: Check your spam folder, confirm the email on your account is correct, and try requesting the statement again after a few minutes.

commonProblems.problem: The PDF won't open — it's asking for a password
commonProblems.solution: The statement is password-protected. Enter the password in the format GTBank specifies in the email that delivered the file.

faqs.question: Is downloading my GTBank statement free?
faqs.answer: Requesting an e-statement through the app or internet banking is typically free; a stamped statement collected at a branch may attract a fee.

faqs.question: How far back can I get?
faqs.answer: You can usually select a custom date range covering several months or more. For very old periods, contact GTBank directly.

faqs.question: Can I use the statement in Automonie?
faqs.answer: Yes. Automonie reads GTBank statements (even password-protected ones) and sorts every transaction into categories automatically.

title: Financial Blindness: Why You Never Know Where Your Money Went
titleTag: Financial Blindness: Where Did Your Money Go?
metaDescription: Financial blindness is spending you cannot account for — small transfers, top-ups and fees that add up. Why it happens in Nigeria, and how to finally see it.
directAnswer: Financial blindness is spending money you cannot account for — not from one big purchase, but a hundred small transfers, top-ups and fees that never felt like spending. The fix is not more discipline; it is simply seeing every naira, so the pattern becomes obvious.

children.text: You earned well this month. You were not reckless. And yet, somehow, the money is gone — and if someone asked you to explain where it went, you could not. That gap, between what you earned and what you can account for, is financial blindness. It is not a character flaw. It is a data problem.
It is never one big purchase

People imagine overspending as a single dramatic mistake. It almost never is. It is a transfer to a friend here, a POS withdrawal there, airtime you topped up twice, a delivery fee, a subscription you forgot you had, a little black tax. None of it felt like spending in the moment. Added together at the end of the month, it is most of your salary.
Why it is worse in Nigeria

Money here moves in ways that are hard to track by memory. You might use three or four apps — a traditional bank, Opay, PalmPay, Moniepoint — and cash on top. Every transfer looks the same in your head. Bank alerts pile up and get ignored. The result is that the single most important number in your financial life, where your money actually goes, is invisible to you.
The real cost of not seeing

You cannot fix what you cannot see. Budgets fail because they are built on a guess. Savings goals slip because the money you meant to set aside quietly leaked out in ways you never noticed. And the stress of not knowing is its own tax — a low background anxiety about money that never quite goes away, even in months you did fine.
How to see clearly, in minutes

The cure for financial blindness is not a stricter budget or more willpower. It is sight. Pull one month of history — download a bank statement or let an app read your SMS alerts — and put every transaction into a real category. The moment you see that transfers took a third of your income, or that food and airtime quietly ate more than your rent, the pattern stops being a mystery. You do not need to judge it. You just need to see it.

That is the entire idea behind Automonie: read your statements and alerts, sort every naira, and show you the truth in seconds. Not to lecture you — just to end the blindness, so the decisions that follow are finally yours to make with your eyes open.

faqs.question: What is financial blindness?
faqs.answer: Financial blindness is being unable to account for where your money went — usually because it left in many small, forgettable transactions rather than one big purchase.

faqs.question: How do I know if I have it?
faqs.answer: If you cannot explain, from memory, where most of last month’s income went, you have it. Almost everyone does until they actually look at the data.

faqs.question: How do I fix it?
faqs.answer: Take one month of transactions — from a statement or your SMS alerts — and sort every one into a category. Seeing the pattern is the fix; an app like Automonie does the sorting for you.
